headline: New contracts slip as infrastructure signings weaken
summary_short: China State Construction's H1 2026 newly signed contracts totaled ¥2.46T, down 1.5% y/y, as infrastructure signings fell 10.8% y/y while housing construction rose 3.7% y/y; Q2 standalone EPS of ¥0.15 fell 54.5% q/q.
summary_long: H1 2026 new contracts signed totaled ¥2.46T (-1.5% y/y). By segment: housing construction contracts ¥1.55T (+3.7% y/y), infrastructure contracts ¥734B (-10.8% y/y) — infrastructure weakness outweighed housing resilience. Q2 standalone EPS of ¥0.15 fell 54.5% q/q from ¥0.33. Confirmed Q1 2026 actuals (not H1) showed revenue of ¥511.85B (-7.85% y/y) and net profit of ¥13.88B (-7.53% y/y); reliable H1-cumulative revenue/profit figures were not obtainable within budget, so they are omitted rather than estimated.
confidence_notes: No edgarCik; shard sourceLink is a Yahoo fallback. Two WebSearch queries found the company's own H1 2026 operating briefing (经营情况简报, a mandatory SSE monthly/interim operating disclosure) with new-contract figures, but not H1 revenue/net profit (only Q1 2026 actuals were confirmed via a separate article). A WebFetch of the Shanghai Securities News (paper.cnstock.com) recap returned no extractable table data; a second WebFetch of the Sina Finance announcement detail page returned garbled/implausible 'operating profit' and 'financial income' figures (internally inconsistent with confirmed Q1 net profit scale — almost certainly a 亿/万-unit misread by the extraction pass) and mislabeled the housing/infrastructure new-contract breakdown as 'revenue'; those figures are therefore NOT used here. New-contract totals and segment breakdown are taken from the original WebSearch's own correctly-parsed synthesis (24,647亿元 total, 15,511亿元 housing, 7,344亿元 infrastructure), cross-checked for internal consistency (housing + infrastructure + other ≈ total). EPS row is the Q2-standalone actual from resolve-earnings-target.mjs's shard KPIs (Yahoo earningsChart).

drivers.explanation: Housing construction contracts rose 3.7% y/y while infrastructure contracts fell 10.8% y/y, and the infrastructure decline outweighed housing's gain in the total.
